docs.title: Cybersecurity Handbook
docs.text:
This handbook turns study notes and lab experience into a connected system for lawful, authorized security assessments. It separates durable concepts from repeatable procedures and case-specific writeups.

Authorization is a prerequisite

Use the operational material only in labs you control or on systems for which you have explicit written authorization. Rules of engagement, safety constraints, and applicable law always take precedence over a playbook.

  • Knowledge

    Concepts, technologies, protocols, trust boundaries, and vulnerability classes.

    Browse knowledge

  • Playbooks

    End-to-end engagement workflows with decision points, evidence, and stop conditions.

    Browse playbooks

  • Techniques

    Focused, reusable procedures tied to preconditions, risks, detection, and remediation.

    Browse techniques

  • Writeups

    Chronological lab narratives that preserve hypotheses, failures, evidence, and lessons.

    Browse writeups

  • Blog

    Dated research notes, learning retrospectives, and analysis.

    Browse the blog

  • Field operations

    Scoping, communications, evidence handling, cleanup, and quality assurance.

    Browse field operations

  • Reporting

    Finding patterns, risk reasoning, remediation, and attack narratives.

    Browse reporting

docs.title: Blog
docs.text:
The blog is for time-oriented articles: research notes, learning retrospectives, tool comparisons, lab lessons, and commentary that has a publication date and authorial voice.

Use Knowledge for canonical explanations, Techniques for reusable testing procedures, and Writeups for case-specific attack paths. A blog post may introduce or summarize those pages, but should link to them instead of becoming their only home.

docs.title: Development
docs.text: This section turns the handbook into a deliberate learning system.

docs.title: Collections
docs.text:
• Role- and domain-based learning roadmaps
  • Certification objective maps
  • Practice plans and lab queues
  • Skill assessments
  • Retrospectives and lessons learned
  • Knowledge-gap backlog

Certification notes should be original and generalized. Map public objectives to your own pages, but do not reproduce proprietary course or exam content. A useful retrospective identifies what changed in your mental model and which handbook pages now need improvement.

docs.title: Field operations
docs.text: Field operations make technical work safe, reviewable, and professionally useful.

docs.title: Collections
docs.text:
• Scoping and rules of engagement
  • Engagement planning and threat modeling
  • Team roles and communications
  • Note-taking and activity logs
  • Evidence acquisition, integrity, and retention
  • Safety, service stability, and emergency stops
  • Artifact inventory and cleanup
  • Peer review and quality assurance

docs.title: Core records
docs.text: For material activity, record timestamp, operator, source, target placeholder, authorization reference, hypothesis, action, observation, evidence location, interpretation, side effects, and cleanup state. Keep sensitive evidence in an approved encrypted store with appropriate retention controls—not in the published handbook.

docs.title: Note-taking and evidence
docs.text: Good notes let another qualified person reconstruct the reasoning without turning the handbook into a repository of sensitive engagement data.

docs.title: Separate the stores
docs.text:
Use three distinct layers:

Layer Purpose Typical contents Publication status Activity log Chronology and accountability Timestamp, operator, action, target reference, result Private Evidence store Proof and protected artifacts Screenshots, exports, logs, packet captures, hashes Private and access-controlled Handbook Sanitized reusable learning Concepts, techniques, playbooks, generalized examples Publishable after review

Do not commit the activity log or evidence store to the handbook repository.

docs.title: Activity record
docs.text:
Capture material activity as it happens:

Timestamp (with timezone):
Operator:
Authorization or ticket reference:
Source and target placeholders:
Hypothesis:
Action:
Observation:
Interpretation:
Evidence reference:
Artifacts or state changes:
Cleanup status:
Next decision:

An observation is what the system returned. An interpretation explains what it may mean. Keeping them separate makes later peer review far easier.

docs.title: Evidence quality
docs.text:
Evidence should be:

  • sufficient to support the claim but minimized to avoid unnecessary data collection;
  • attributable to the relevant system, identity, time, and action;
  • reproducible when safe and permitted;
  • stored with access, encryption, integrity, and retention appropriate to its classification;
  • referenced consistently from notes and reports;
  • redacted only on a working copy when the original must be preserved.

Hashing can help demonstrate that a file has not changed, but it does not prove who collected it, whether the source was trustworthy, or whether the conclusion is correct. Preserve context.

docs.title: Screenshots
docs.text: Capture the smallest useful region while retaining enough context to identify the application state and result. Hide unrelated personal or sensitive information. Accompany screenshots with text because images alone are difficult to search, compare, and make accessible.

docs.title: Commands and output
docs.text: Record the actual command in the private activity log, its relevant version, execution context, exit status, and minimally necessary output. In the handbook, replace environment values with consistent placeholders and describe any side effects.

docs.title: Sanitization before publication
docs.text:
Search for and remove:

  • credentials, tokens, keys, cookies, and connection strings;
  • client and employee names, email addresses, and personal information;
  • public and private addresses tied to a real engagement;
  • internal hostnames, domains, tenant IDs, account IDs, and repository URLs;
  • screenshots with browser history, notifications, terminal prompts, or hidden metadata;
  • flags and restricted lab or course content;
  • dates, filenames, or narratives that can indirectly identify a client.

When risk is meaningful, use independent review: the person who sanitized the page should not be its only reviewer.

docs.title: Knowledge
docs.text: Knowledge pages explain systems, protocols, trust boundaries, and security properties. They answer why a technique works and should remain useful after a particular tool or command changes.

docs.title: Areas
docs.text:
• Fundamentals: networking, operating systems, cryptography, authentication, and scripting.
  • Technologies: application and infrastructure platforms encountered during assessments.
  • Vulnerability classes: recurring root causes, security impact, detection, and remediation.

docs.title: Expected shape
docs.text: A strong article includes a mental model, components and trust boundaries, normal behavior, security assumptions, common failure modes, testing implications, defensive visibility, mitigations, and primary references. Use the knowledge article template.

docs.title: Fundamentals
docs.text: Foundational subjects support every specialization. Add one focused page per concept rather than one enormous page per domain.

docs.title: Planned collections
docs.text:
• Networking and common protocols
  • Linux, Windows, and macOS internals
  • Cryptography and key management
  • Identity, authentication, and authorization
  • Programming, scripting, and data formats
  • Virtualization, containers, and distributed systems
  • Logging, telemetry, and security controls

Connect each concept to technologies that implement it and techniques that depend on it.

docs.title: Technologies
docs.text: Technology pages model a platform before discussing how to assess it. Describe components, identities, data flows, trust boundaries, administrative surfaces, expected telemetry, and security controls.

docs.title: Planned collections
docs.text:
• Active Directory and enterprise identity
  • Web applications and browsers
  • APIs and service-to-service authentication
  • Relational and non-relational databases
  • AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud
  • Containers and Kubernetes
  • Email and collaboration platforms
  • Wireless networks
  • Mobile and thick-client applications

Tool-specific instructions belong in Techniques or Reference; a technology page should explain the platform even when tools change.

docs.title: Vulnerability classes
docs.text: Organize vulnerabilities by underlying failure, not only by product or scanner label. This makes knowledge transferable.

docs.title: Suggested page families
docs.text:
• Input handling and injection
  • Authentication and session management
  • Authorization and access control
  • Unsafe deserialization and object binding
  • File and path handling
  • Cryptographic design and implementation
  • Secrets management
  • Memory safety
  • Race conditions and concurrency
  • Business-logic abuse
  • Security misconfiguration and exposed management planes
  • Supply-chain and dependency risk

Each page should cover root cause, preconditions, impact, safe validation, false positives, observable behavior, prevention, remediation, and authoritative references.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text: Methodology defines the principles and phase model behind an assessment. It is broader than a playbook: it explains coverage, assurance, evidence standards, and how conclusions are reached.

docs.title: Planned methods
docs.text:
• Network penetration testing
  • Web application and API assessment
  • Active Directory assessment
  • Cloud security assessment
  • Adversary simulation and red-team operations
  • Purple-team exercises
  • Social-engineering assessment
  • Physical security assessment

docs.title: Minimum method components
docs.text: Every methodology should define objectives, inputs, coverage model, phases, test-selection logic, evidence threshold, risk controls, exit criteria, and deliverables. Map relevant controls to recognized frameworks without treating a checklist as proof of security.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
Copy the template that matches the page's purpose, then remove instructions and empty sections that do not apply.

  • Knowledge article — explains a concept or technology.
  • Technique — tests one reusable hypothesis.
  • Playbook — coordinates an end-to-end assessment workflow.
  • Writeup — records one lab or challenge journey.
  • Blog post — publishes a dated article or learning retrospective.
  • Finding — communicates an evidenced security issue.

Templates are deliberately structured around reasoning, authorization, safety, evidence, defensive visibility, and cleanup.

docs.title: Blog post template
docs.text:
The following block is the starting point for a file under docs/blog/posts/. Blog posts remain unpublished while draft is true.

---
date:
  created: 2026-09-26
  updated: 2026-09-26
draft: true
categories:
  - Learning
tags:
  - replace-me
description: One sentence used in previews and search results.
---

# Specific, outcome-oriented title

Open with the useful conclusion or question. Give readers enough context to decide whether the article is relevant.

<!-- more -->

## Context

Explain the lab, research question, or learning objective without exposing sensitive or restricted information.

## What I observed

Separate verified observations from interpretations. Use sanitized examples and link to evidence only when it is safe and publishable.

## Why it matters

Connect the observation to a broader mental model, defensive implication, or assessment practice.

## Practical lessons

State what should change in a methodology, technique, control, or learning plan.

## Related handbook pages

- Knowledge:
- Techniques:
- Playbooks:
- Writeups:

## References

Prefer primary sources and record enough detail for readers to verify the claims.

docs.title: Executive summary
docs.text: State the condition, affected scope, and business consequence in plain language. Do not exaggerate beyond the evidence.

docs.title: Affected scope
docs.text: List systems, components, roles, or data classes using sanitized identifiers in reusable library entries.

docs.title: Description and root cause
docs.text: Explain what is wrong, why it exists, and which trust or control assumption failed.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text: Document the minimal evidence needed to support the claim. In a live report, reference the protected evidence store rather than embedding unnecessary sensitive data.

docs.title: Reproduction or validation
docs.text: Provide deterministic, authorized validation steps with prerequisites, expected results, risks, and cleanup.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: Separate demonstrated impact from plausible impact. Describe affected confidentiality, integrity, availability, safety, or business process.

docs.title: Likelihood and severity rationale
docs.text: Record environmental preconditions, attacker position, reliability, existing controls, exposure, and the selected rating method.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
1. Immediate containment, if necessary
  2. Root-cause correction
  3. Defense-in-depth improvements
  4. Monitoring and detection improvements

Include ownership hints and practical verification criteria without prescribing one product unless necessary.

docs.title: Retest criteria
docs.text: State what evidence would demonstrate that the issue is fixed and that related paths are closed.

docs.title: References
docs.text: Prefer authoritative standards, vendor guidance, and stable vulnerability identifiers.

docs.title: Topic name
docs.text: One paragraph stating what the topic is and why it matters.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text: Explain the simplest useful model. Define important terms before using them.

docs.title: Components and data flow
docs.text: Identify actors, services, identities, data, protocols, and boundaries.

docs.title: Trust and security assumptions
docs.text:
• What is trusted?
  • What must remain secret or intact?
  • Where are authorization decisions made?
  • Which assumptions commonly fail?

docs.title: Normal operation
docs.text: Describe the legitimate lifecycle or protocol flow.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text: Describe recurring weaknesses by root cause. Link to canonical vulnerability-class pages.

docs.title: Assessment relevance
docs.text: Explain what an authorized assessor would want to establish and which observations matter. Link to techniques rather than duplicating procedures.

docs.title: Defensive visibility
docs.text: Describe useful logs, alerts, state changes, and investigation evidence.

docs.title: Hardening and remediation
docs.text: Prioritize design fixes and durable controls over signatures or tool-specific blocking.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: Record misleading shortcuts and explain the more accurate model.

docs.title: Related material
docs.text:
• Techniques:
  • Playbooks:
  • Writeups:

docs.title: References
docs.text: Prefer standards, vendor documentation, and original research. Record an access date for content likely to change.

docs.title: Playbook name
docs.text:
Authorization

Written authorization and current rules of engagement are required. The playbook never overrides scope, law, safety constraints, or an operator's duty to stop.

docs.title: Purpose and outcomes
docs.text: Define the assessment type, intended audience, success criteria, and deliverables.

docs.title: Inputs and prerequisites
docs.text:
• Scope and rules of engagement
  • Test window and source infrastructure
  • Accounts, access, and assumptions
  • Contacts and emergency procedures
  • Evidence and data-handling requirements

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: List explicitly prohibited actions, rate limits, fragile systems, third-party dependencies, and approval gates.

docs.title: 1. Prepare
docs.text: Confirm authorization, instrumentation, communications, time synchronization, storage, and rollback capability.

docs.title: 2. Establish the environment
docs.text: Collect the minimum context needed to choose safe tests. Record unknowns as hypotheses.

docs.title: 3. Test prioritized hypotheses
docs.text:
Link to individual Technique pages. For each decision point, state:

  • observation;
  • interpretation;
  • next safe test;
  • evidence required;
  • stop or approval condition.

docs.title: 4. Validate impact
docs.text: Use the least harmful proof that meets the engagement objective. Do not expand access merely because it is technically possible.

docs.title: 5. Clean up and restore
docs.text: Reconcile the artifact inventory, remove authorized test artifacts, verify state, and record exceptions.

docs.title: 6. Analyze and report
docs.text: Connect evidence to root causes, affected scope, attack paths, risk, remediation, and retest criteria.

docs.title: Decision points
docs.text: Condition Meaning Next action Approval required?

docs.title: Evidence checklist
docs.text:
• Activity log is complete
  • Claims have supporting evidence
  • Sensitive data is minimized and protected
  • Attack-path links are time-ordered
  • Cleanup is documented

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text: List the expected report, evidence package, debrief, cleanup confirmation, and follow-up actions.

docs.title: Technique name
docs.text:
Authorization

Use only in an isolated lab or where the rules of engagement explicitly authorize this test.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: State the security hypothesis and what a successful test establishes.

docs.title: Preconditions
docs.text:
• Required access and privileges
  • In-scope platform or version assumptions
  • Required configuration or environmental state
  • Authorization constraints

docs.title: Safety and stop conditions
docs.text: Describe service, data, identity, monitoring, or availability risks. State when to stop and escalate.

docs.title: Underlying concept
docs.text: Explain why the technique can work and link to the relevant Knowledge page.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text: Use numbered steps. Keep placeholders explicit and describe expected behavior before commands.

docs.title: Expected observations
docs.text: Observation Interpretation Confidence Next question

docs.title: Evidence to capture
docs.text:
• Timestamp and operator
  • Input and relevant configuration
  • Minimal output proving the result
  • Environment and version information
  • Side effects or artifacts

docs.title: False positives and limitations
docs.text: Explain alternative interpretations, environmental differences, and what the test cannot prove.

docs.title: Detection opportunities
docs.text: Describe relevant telemetry, state changes, and high-signal correlations.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Describe root-cause remediation, compensating controls, and verification.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text: List every artifact or state change and how to verify restoration.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: List safer or more reliable ways to answer the same hypothesis.

docs.title: References and related pages
docs.text:
• Knowledge:
  • Playbooks:
  • Writeups:
  • Primary references:

docs.title: Target or lab name
docs.text:
Publication check

Confirm the platform permits publication, the target is retired where required, and the page contains no flags, proprietary content, secrets, or personal data.

Draft location

Create generated drafts under docs/writeups/drafts/<source>/. Move them into the published writeups tree only after human review and publication approval.

docs.title: Objective and scope
docs.text: State the learning objective, lab source, allowed actions, and spoiler level.

docs.title: Initial hypotheses
docs.text: Record what you expected before testing and why.

docs.title: Enumeration and observations
docs.text:
Keep observations separate from conclusions. Record enough context to understand later decisions.

Observation Hypothesis Validation Result

docs.title: Attack path
docs.text: Describe the successful path chronologically and link reusable steps to Technique pages.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text: Use sanitized excerpts that prove important transitions without leaking flags or restricted material.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Explain the trust or security failure that enabled the path.

docs.title: Failed approaches
docs.text: Record plausible attempts that failed, why they failed, and what distinguished them from the successful path.

docs.title: Alternative paths
docs.text: Describe alternatives you verified or have clearly marked as unverified hypotheses.

docs.title: Defensive perspective
docs.text: Identify relevant prevention, logging, detection, containment, and investigation opportunities.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Address root cause and attack-path dependencies, not just the final symptom.

docs.title: Lessons learned
docs.text:
• What changed in the mental model?
  • Which assumptions were wrong?
  • Which action was noisy, unsafe, or inefficient?
  • What should be practiced again?

  • New or updated Techniques:
  • Playbook changes:

docs.title: Playbooks
docs.text: Playbooks are the handbook's engagement tutorials. They coordinate many techniques in a safe order and explain what to do when observations change the plan.

docs.title: Planned playbooks
docs.text:
• External attack-surface assessment
  • Internal network assessment
  • Assumed-breach assessment
  • Web application assessment
  • API assessment
  • Active Directory assessment
  • Cloud assessment
  • Post-exploitation validation and cleanup

docs.title: Design rules
docs.text:
A playbook must include authorization checks, prerequisites, success criteria, phases, decision points, evidence requirements, stop conditions, cleanup, and deliverables. Link to technique pages for detailed procedures instead of embedding a long command list.

Use the playbook template.

docs.title: Authorized assessment lifecycle
docs.text:
This playbook is the common spine for more specialized playbooks. It organizes an assessment around explicit authorization, testable hypotheses, proportional validation, evidence, cleanup, and communication.

Authorization

Written authorization and the current rules of engagement control every phase. If the observed environment differs materially from the approved scope, stop the affected activity and resolve the discrepancy.

docs.title: 1. Define the engagement
docs.text:
Establish the business objective before choosing tools or tests.

  • Identify the decision the assessment must support.
  • Name in-scope systems, identities, facilities, applications, APIs, cloud tenants, and third parties.
  • Record explicit exclusions, prohibited actions, rate limits, and production constraints.
  • Define the assessment type: vulnerability assessment, penetration test, assumed breach, adversary simulation, or another clearly scoped exercise.
  • Agree on success criteria, evidence requirements, reporting format, and retest expectations.

docs.title: Exit criteria
docs.text: Do not proceed until authorization, scope, dates, operators, contacts, data handling, emergency stop, and cleanup ownership are documented.

docs.title: 2. Prepare the operation
docs.text:
Create the minimum infrastructure and records necessary for safe work.

  • Confirm operator identities and approved test sources.
  • Synchronize clocks and establish an activity-log format.
  • Test communication and emergency escalation paths.
  • Prepare approved encrypted evidence storage.
  • Identify fragile services and monitoring expectations.
  • Establish an artifact inventory and naming convention.
  • Validate that test accounts, lab replicas, backups, or rollback methods work where applicable.

docs.title: 3. Model the environment
docs.text:
Build an initial picture using provided documentation and low-impact observations. Treat unknowns as explicit hypotheses.

Question Evidence sought Why it changes the plan What assets and trust boundaries exist? Inventories, diagrams, observed services Prevents accidental scope expansion Which identities and privilege tiers exist? Role definitions, approved account context Guides authorization testing safely Where is sensitive data processed? Data flows and classifications Controls evidence collection and impact validation Which controls should observe testing? Logging and detection coverage Supports purple-team and detection objectives

Update the model when evidence contradicts it. Do not force observations into the initial plan.

docs.title: 4. Prioritize hypotheses
docs.text:
Turn the threat model and observations into testable statements. Prioritize by expected impact, exposure, plausibility, coverage value, and operational risk.

For each hypothesis, define:

  1. the precondition being tested;
  2. the least disruptive validation method;
  3. the expected positive and negative observations;
  4. the evidence threshold;
  5. side effects and cleanup;
  6. the stop or approval condition.

Use specialized Technique pages for procedures. A failed tool command is not a negative security result unless the technique and its assumptions were validated.

docs.title: 5. Execute and adapt
docs.text:
Work from low-impact discovery toward narrowly scoped validation. Maintain an activity log while testing, not after the fact.

After each material observation, ask:

  • Does this remain in scope?
  • Does it change the risk or safety model?
  • Is the result an observation, an inference, or demonstrated impact?
  • What is the next smallest test that reduces uncertainty?
  • Is additional approval required?
  • What artifacts were created?

Pause when scope is ambiguous, safety assumptions fail, sensitive data appears unexpectedly, a third party is involved, or service stability changes.

docs.title: 6. Validate impact proportionally
docs.text:
Demonstrate only the impact needed to support the objective. Prefer reversible proofs and synthetic data. Avoid collecting real data, changing business records, disrupting services, or expanding privileges when a smaller proof is sufficient.

Record both demonstrated impact and credible but untested impact. Never present the latter as observed fact.

docs.title: 7. Preserve evidence
docs.text:
For every conclusion, retain the minimum evidence that establishes who, what, when, where, and how. Follow the note-taking and evidence standard.

Evidence should be attributable, time-ordered, integrity-protected where required, and stored according to the engagement's classification and retention rules.

docs.title: 8. Clean up and reconcile
docs.text:
Compare the artifact inventory with the activity log. Remove approved testing artifacts, restore changed state, revoke temporary access, and document anything that cannot be removed.

Cleanup is complete only after verification. An attempted deletion is not proof of restoration.

docs.title: 9. Analyze and report
docs.text:
Group symptoms by root cause and connect individual findings into attack paths where the evidence supports it. Each material claim should trace to protected evidence.

Reports should distinguish:

  • observed condition;
  • demonstrated impact;
  • plausible additional impact;
  • affected scope and uncertainty;
  • root cause;
  • prioritized remediation;
  • retest criteria.

docs.title: 10. Close and improve
docs.text:
Confirm evidence transfer or destruction, outstanding cleanup, retest ownership, and final communications. Conduct a retrospective and promote reusable lessons into the handbook:

  • concepts into Knowledge;
  • focused procedures into Techniques;
  • workflow improvements into Playbooks;
  • communication patterns into Reporting;
  • diagnostic shortcuts into Reference.

docs.title: Completion checklist
docs.text:
• Scope and authorization remained current
  • Material actions are represented in the activity log
  • Claims trace to sufficient evidence
  • Sensitive data collection was minimized
  • Artifacts and state changes were reconciled
  • Findings include root cause and retest criteria
  • Residual risk and uncertainty are explicit
  • Reusable learning was extracted into the handbook

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Reference material is optimized for retrieval during study or an authorized engagement. It supports understanding; it does not replace it.

docs.title: Planned collections
docs.text:
• Pre-engagement, testing, cleanup, and reporting checklists
  • Decision trees and diagnostic questions
  • Command and tool quick references
  • Ports, protocols, file formats, and identifiers
  • Troubleshooting guides
  • Curated primary references and further reading

Commands should state platform, version, placeholders, expected behavior, side effects, and last verification date. Do not create context-free payload dumps.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text: Reporting translates technical evidence into decisions. Maintain reusable structures, but adapt every finding to the actual environment and demonstrated impact.

docs.title: Collections
docs.text:
• Finding library
  • Executive communication
  • Technical evidence and reproduction
  • Risk-rating guidance
  • Remediation patterns
  • Attack-path narratives
  • Report review checklists

docs.title: Finding quality
docs.text:
A finding should state the affected scope, condition, root cause, evidence, demonstrated or plausible impact, likelihood reasoning, severity rationale, actionable remediation, and retest criteria. Avoid scanner prose and unsupported worst-case claims.

Use the finding template.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text: The handbook is a publishing layer, not an evidence store or scratchpad. Write raw notes elsewhere, remove sensitive information, and promote only durable, lawful material into this repository.

docs.title: First steps
docs.text:
1. Read Ethics and authorization.
  2. Learn where content belongs in the Handbook map.
  3. Follow the Authoring guide.
  4. Copy the appropriate page from Templates.
  5. Run mkdocs build --strict before opening a pull request.

docs.title: Quality bar
docs.text: A useful page states its assumptions, separates observation from inference, records how information was verified, links to primary references, includes defensive context, and carries a review date when its accuracy can decay.

docs.title: Page lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Capture private working notes.
  2. Remove secrets, client identifiers, personal data, and prohibited material.
  3. Create a writeup or draft article from the appropriate template.
  4. Extract reusable concepts and procedures instead of duplicating them.
  5. Validate commands and claims in an isolated lab.
  6. Review the rendered page and run a strict build.
  7. Set last_verified on content whose behavior changes over time.

docs.title: Front matter
docs.text:
Use YAML front matter for discovery and maintenance:

---
title: Descriptive page title
description: One-sentence summary.
tags: [active-directory, authentication]
status: draft
last_verified: 2026-09-26
---

Recommended status values are draft, reviewed, verified, and deprecated. Tags should describe the technology, platform, assessment type, or framework—not repeat the section name.

docs.title: Writing standards
docs.text:
• Start with the outcome or mental model.
  • State preconditions and scope explicitly.
  • Distinguish facts, observations, hypotheses, and conclusions.
  • Explain why a step works; do not publish unexplained command collections.
  • Prefer vendor documentation, standards, and original research as sources.
  • Include detection, prevention, and remediation alongside offensive material.
  • Record side effects, reliability concerns, cleanup, and stop conditions.
  • Use placeholders such as TARGET_IP, DOMAIN, and USERNAME; never real client values.
  • Link to a canonical concept or technique instead of copying it.
  • Do not claim verification that you did not perform.

docs.title: Commands and output
docs.text: Use fenced code blocks with a language identifier. Separate commands from representative output, and redact environment-specific values. Explain destructive or disruptive behavior before showing a command.

docs.title: Adding a page
docs.text:
Copy a file from Templates, rename it with lowercase hyphenated words, and add it to nav in mkdocs.yml. Run:

mkdocs build --strict

Strict mode turns documentation warnings into build failures so navigation and links do not silently decay.

docs.title: Ethics and authorization
docs.text: Technical capability is not authorization. Use this handbook only in environments you own, intentionally provided training labs, or engagements covered by explicit written permission.

docs.title: Before testing
docs.text:
Confirm at minimum:

  • named in-scope systems, identities, locations, and third parties;
  • permitted test types, dates, source infrastructure, and operator identities;
  • prohibited actions and production-safety constraints;
  • data access, retention, encryption, and destruction requirements;
  • escalation contacts, emergency stop procedures, and reporting cadence;
  • whether persistence, social engineering, physical access, denial of service, or data movement is permitted;
  • cleanup and evidence-handling expectations.

docs.title: During testing
docs.text: Choose the least harmful validation that proves the finding. Stop when conditions exceed authorization, a safety assumption fails, sensitive data appears unexpectedly, or system stability is at risk. Record enough evidence for reproducibility without collecting unnecessary data.

docs.title: Before publication
docs.text:
Never publish secrets, client identifiers, personal data, private network details, live targets, confidential evidence, or material restricted by a lab, course, certification, employer, or contract. Sanitization should be reviewed by someone who did not write the original notes when the stakes warrant it.

Warning

A private GitHub repository does not make its Pages site private in every plan or configuration. Treat any Pages deployment as publicly accessible unless you have independently verified access controls.

docs.title: Handbook map
docs.text:
The site uses a small number of top-level content types. Folders below them can grow organically; avoid adding a new top-level section when an existing content type fits.

docs/
├── start-here/                 # Orientation, governance, and authoring rules
├── knowledge/
│   ├── fundamentals/           # Networks, operating systems, crypto, programming
│   ├── technologies/           # AD, web, APIs, cloud, containers, databases
│   └── vulnerability-classes/  # Root causes and recurring weakness patterns
├── methodology/                # Assessment standards and phase models
├── playbooks/                  # End-to-end, decision-oriented workflows
├── techniques/                 # One reusable testing hypothesis per page
├── writeups/                   # HTB, OSCP-style labs, CTFs, personal labs
├── blog/posts/                 # Dated research notes and retrospectives
├── field-operations/           # Scope, evidence, safety, cleanup, communications
├── reporting/                  # Findings, risk, remediation, executive narratives
├── reference/                  # Checklists, decision trees, quick lookup material
├── development/                # Learning plans, certification maps, retrospectives
└── page-templates/             # Canonical starting points for new pages

docs.title: Planned taxonomy
docs.text:
Use these as subfolders when there is enough content to justify them. A folder should generally have an index.md that explains its scope.

Area Suggested subdivisions Fundamentals Networking, operating systems, cryptography, authentication, programming and scripting Technologies Active Directory, web applications, APIs, databases, cloud, containers and Kubernetes, wireless, thick clients Methodology Penetration testing, red team, web, Active Directory, cloud, social engineering, physical, purple team Playbooks External, internal, assumed breach, web, AD, cloud, API, post-engagement cleanup Techniques Discovery, initial access, execution, persistence, privilege escalation, credential access, lateral movement, collection, command and control, defense evasion Writeups Hack The Box machines/challenges/academy, Proving Grounds, PortSwigger, OSCP-style labs, CTFs, personal labs Blog Research notes, learning retrospectives, tool analysis, methodology commentary Field operations Scope and ROE, planning, communications, evidence, note-taking, safety, cleanup, QA Reporting Finding library, executive writing, technical writing, risk rating, remediation, attack narratives Reference Checklists, decision trees, commands, ports and protocols, troubleshooting, further reading Development Certification maps, practice plans, skill assessments, lessons learned

docs.title: Where should a page go?
docs.text:
• If it explains a system or root cause, put it in Knowledge.
  • If it tests one narrowly defined hypothesis, put it in Techniques.
  • If it coordinates a complete assessment, put it in Playbooks.
  • If it records one target or challenge, put it in Writeups.
  • If it is a dated narrative or analysis, put it in the Blog.
  • If it governs how an engagement is run, put it in Field operations.
  • If it helps communicate a result, put it in Reporting.
  • If it is optimized for lookup rather than learning, put it in Reference.

Prefer links over duplication. A writeup should point to a reusable technique, and that technique should point to the knowledge that explains it.

docs.title: LLM-assisted authoring
docs.text: An LLM can accelerate structure, editing, cross-linking, and extraction of reusable lessons. It should not decide whether sensitive material is safe to publish, manufacture missing evidence, or publish without review.

docs.title: 1. Create a private inbox
docs.text:
The .drafts/ directory is ignored by Git:

mkdir -p .drafts

Place raw or partially sanitized notes there. Do not assume that ignore rules protect the content from an external LLM service; they only prevent ordinary Git tracking.

docs.title: 2. Ask the repository-aware LLM
docs.text:
For a writeup:

Read AGENTS.md and prompts/create-writeup.md. Turn
.drafts/example-machine.md into a detailed Hack The Box writeup.
Keep it unpublished, do not invent missing evidence, sanitize all
environment values, and run the strict documentation build.

For a blog post:

Read AGENTS.md and prompts/create-blog-post.md. Turn
.drafts/kerberos-lessons.md into a blog post for intermediate readers.
The main takeaway is that protocol understanding is more durable than
memorizing tool syntax. Keep the post as a draft and run the strict build.

Repository-aware tools such as Codex will automatically receive the rules in AGENTS.md. With a general chat LLM, paste the relevant prompt file and only the sanitized source material it needs.

Generated writeups are placed under docs/writeups/drafts/. MkDocs shows them during local preview with a draft marker and excludes them from production builds. Blog posts use their own draft: true metadata for the same publish/preview separation.

docs.title: 3. Review the diff
docs.text:
Check every generated statement against the notes and source references. In particular, review:

  • commands and version-specific behavior;
  • claims of successful access or demonstrated impact;
  • citations, CVE identifiers, and framework mappings;
  • flags, credentials, cookies, tokens, internal names, addresses, and screenshots;
  • platform restrictions and copyrighted course or exam material;
  • cleanup, detection, remediation, and uncertainty.

docs.title: 4. Preview locally
docs.text:
source .venv/bin/activate
mkdocs serve

Draft blog posts appear during local preview because draft_on_serve is enabled. They are excluded from the production build.

docs.title: 5. Publish deliberately
docs.text:
For a reviewed blog post, change:

draft: true

to:

draft: false

For a writeup, confirm the platform permits publication, move it from docs/writeups/drafts/<source>/ to docs/writeups/<source>/, set its status appropriately, and change publication_allowed only after that check. Add it to mkdocs.yml when it belongs in the main navigation. Run:

mkdocs build --strict

Commit the generated page, any intentional cross-links, and navigation changes. Never commit .drafts/.

docs.title: What the LLM should do well
docs.text:
• apply the correct template and front matter;
  • turn chronology into a readable narrative;
  • distinguish observations from conclusions;
  • identify missing evidence instead of filling gaps;
  • extract reusable knowledge and technique candidates;
  • suggest internal links and primary references;
  • improve remediation and defensive perspective;
  • run structural validation.

docs.title: What remains a human decision
docs.text:
• whether the material can legally and contractually be published;
  • whether sanitization is sufficient;
  • whether a factual or operational claim is correct;
  • whether an assessment action was authorized;
  • whether a draft is ready to become public.

docs.title: API automation later
docs.text: The prompts are provider-neutral. They can later be wrapped in a local script or CI workflow using a chosen LLM API, but that decision should follow a data-flow review: which notes leave the machine, which provider receives them, how requests are retained, where API keys live, and who approves publication. Keep automatic generation and automatic publication as separate steps.

docs.title: Techniques
docs.text: A technique is a focused, reusable way to test one security hypothesis. It is smaller than a playbook and independent of any one lab.

docs.title: Suggested taxonomy
docs.text:
• Discovery and enumeration
  • Initial access
  • Execution
  • Persistence
  • Privilege escalation
  • Credential and secret access
  • Lateral movement
  • Collection and impact validation
  • Command and control
  • Defense evasion

Framework mappings such as MITRE ATT&CK are metadata, not the primary folder structure. One technique may span platforms or map to several framework entries.

Every technique should document preconditions, safe validation, expected evidence, interpretation, side effects, detection, remediation, alternatives, cleanup, and a verification date. Use the technique template.

docs.title: Writeups
docs.text: Writeups preserve the reasoning path for a specific lab, machine, or challenge. They complement reusable knowledge; they should not become the knowledge base themselves.

docs.title: Suggested collections
docs.text:
• Hack The Box machines, challenges, and Academy exercises
  • Proving Grounds and OSCP-style practice labs
  • PortSwigger Web Security Academy labs
  • CTF challenges
  • Personal and purpose-built labs

docs.title: Preserve the learning
docs.text:
Record initial hypotheses, observations, attack path, evidence, failed approaches, root cause, defensive perspective, remediation, and knowledge gaps. Then extract reusable material into Knowledge, Techniques, Playbooks, or Reporting.

Respect platform rules and copyright. Do not publish active-machine solutions, flags, proprietary exam material, or restricted course content. Use the writeup template.
